title: K-Row — か き く け こ

points.name: か
points.explanation: The syllable か combines the 'k' consonant with the vowel あ, producing a crisp 'ka' sound exactly as in 'karate' or 'karma'. The 'k' in Japanese is unaspirated — meaning there's no puff of air after it, unlike the English 'k' in 'key' (put your hand in front of your mouth and feel the difference between English 'key' versus Japanese か). This slight difference gives Japanese its cleaner, crisper consonant sound. か is one of the most common syllables in Japanese and appears in countless everyday words, including the question particle か that turns any statement into a yes-or-no question.
rules: Produce the 'k' without a puff of air — hold your hand in front of your mouth and aim for no breath feeling on your palm.
Follow immediately with the open 'ah' vowel — no pause between the consonant and vowel.
か is also the question particle: adding か to the end of a sentence makes it a yes-or-no question.

points.name: き
points.explanation: The syllable き combines 'k' with the vowel い to make a bright, forward 'kee' sound — like saying 'key' but with an unaspirated 'k' (no breath puff). Your tongue touches the roof of your mouth near the back to form the 'k', then springs forward and up to produce the 'ee' vowel. き is extremely common in Japanese; it appears in words for tree (き), season (きせつ), and 'to listen' (きく), among hundreds of other everyday terms. It also forms part of the grammar for past-tense adjectives.
rules: The 'k' is unaspirated — softer than English 'key', with no puff of air.
Let the vowel fully ring out as a clean 'ee' — don't clip it short.
き can appear alone as a word meaning 'tree' or 'spirit / energy' depending on context.

points.name: く
points.explanation: The syllable く combines 'k' with the vowel う — remember that Japanese う is produced with relaxed, unrounded lips, so く sounds different from English 'coo' or 'queue'. Think of it as a clean 'k' followed by that characteristic Japanese 'oo-without-rounding'. く appears in extremely common Japanese words and grammar, including the verb ending that turns adjectives into adverbs (おそく means 'slowly', from おそい 'slow'). It's also part of the word for 'nine' (く or きゅう), used in counting.
rules: Keep lips relaxed and flat after the 'k' — don't round them into an English 'coo' shape.
The 'k' is unaspirated, so no breath puff.
く frequently appears as an adverb-forming suffix on adjectives.

points.name: け
points.explanation: The syllable け pairs the 'k' consonant with the vowel え, producing a sound like the 'ke' in 'kettle' or 'keg'. As with all Japanese 'k' sounds, keep the consonant unaspirated — cleaner than English, without the small burst of air. け itself appears as part of many useful Japanese words and also shows up in the casual speech pattern けど ('but / however'), which you'll hear all the time in conversation once you start watching Japanese media.
rules: Same clean, unaspirated 'k' as all other か-row characters.
The vowel is a pure 'eh' sound — like the 'e' in 'bed', not the 'ay' in 'cake'.
Watch the shape of け carefully — don't confuse it with は or ほ.

points.name: こ
points.explanation: The syllable こ combines 'k' with the vowel お, creating a sound like the 'co' in 'cold' or 'coat' — but again with the unaspirated Japanese 'k'. こ is one of the most versatile syllables in Japanese: it appears in the demonstrative pronouns (この 'this', ここ 'here', これ 'this thing'), in everyday nouns like こえ (voice) and こい (love / carp), and even as a word on its own meaning 'child' in certain contexts. Mastering こ opens up a huge swath of basic Japanese vocabulary.
rules: Unaspirated 'k' as always — clean consonant, no breath puff.
Round your lips slightly for the 'o' vowel, then stop cleanly without gliding.
こ is the basis for 'here' (ここ), 'this' (これ/この), and many other key demonstratives.

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does this character make?
chapterPractice.explanation: か makes the 'ka' sound, like the 'ka' in 'karate'. It's the first character of the K-row.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which character makes the 'ko' sound (like 'co' in 'cold')?
chapterPractice.explanation: こ makes the 'ko' sound. Notice its two simple horizontal strokes — one of the most recognizable hiragana characters.
かお (kao) means 'face'. It uses か (ka) + お (o). You'll use this word when talking about people's expressions.
いく (iku) means 'to go'. It's one of the first verbs learners pick up, pairing い (i) + く (ku).
